lesson.menu_title: Sorry, Could You Say That Again?
lesson.menu_desc: A fast video call with a supplier in India: stopping politely, asking for clarification and recapping the dates -- Could you tell me why... / Do you know whether... -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Sorry, Could You Say That Again?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Julius Cesar do Nascimento | Lesson 3 -- Sorry, Could You Say That Again?
lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions and clarification requests: Could you tell me why the shipment is late? Do you know whether it is delayed? I was wondering if you could... (opening + question word or if / whether + subject + verb, no do / does / did)

listenings.text: Customers often ask me why their shipment is late, and the honest answer is that it's usually not one big problem. It's five small ones. A ship leaves a day late. A container is checked at customs. A truck driver is sick. Each problem adds a few days, and suddenly the lead time is three weeks longer. So my advice is this. When you talk to your logistics team, don't just ask whether the shipment is late. Ask where it is right now, what the next step is, and who is responsible for it. And at the end of every call, recap the dates and confirm them by email. Most delays don't come from the ocean. They come from a misunderstanding between two people who were too polite to ask a second question.

I'm an engineer in Stuttgart, and I use English every day, but it's not my first language. For years, I was afraid to say that I didn't understand. In meetings with Americans, I just smiled and nodded, and later I asked a colleague what the decision was. Then one day I nodded at the wrong moment, and I agreed to a delivery date that was impossible. That was an expensive mistake. Since then, I always have a few sentences ready. Sorry, could you say that again? Could you tell me what you mean by that? Do you know if the date is fixed? Nobody has ever been annoyed. In fact, the native speakers usually slow down and thank me, because other people at the table didn't understand either.

I train American managers who work with international teams, and I always start with the same message. If the people at your table don't understand you, it's not only their problem. It's yours. Native speakers talk too fast, they use idioms, and they make jokes about baseball. So I teach them three habits. First, slow down, especially with numbers and dates. Second, avoid idioms. Instead of saying that a price is in the ballpark, say that the price is close. Third, check understanding. Don't ask, do you understand? Nobody says no to that question. Ask, could you tell me what the next step is for your team? If the answer is clear, you're done. If it isn't, you've just avoided a very expensive misunderstanding.
